arc_intro:
FQ-156 — Priya Nair (Cloud Architect)

Good work on the subnets. Now let's talk about something FoodQuick has never actually tested: what happens when an entire Availability Zone goes down.

foodquick-orders-db is still Multi-AZ OFF — we noted that back in C3.1 and never came back to it. And the order-service Auto Scaling Group technically spans two AZs, but I want you to check the actual min/desired numbers before assuming that means anything. A lot of teams THINK they're covered because a resource is 'in 2 AZs' without checking whether it can actually survive losing one of them.

Assume ap-south-1b disappears for an hour. Walk me through what actually happens today.

— Priya
arc_outro:
Priya Nair — FQ-156 update:

foodquick-orders-db is Multi-AZ now — standby in a second AZ, automatic failover, same endpoint, no app changes needed if the primary ever goes down. And the ASG is actually sized to survive losing an AZ now, not just technically 'spanning' one.

The capacity error you hit during the AZ-failure test was a good one to see for real — AWS not always having capacity exactly when and where you need it is a real, ongoing operational fact, not a one-time bug. Spreading across a third AZ and adding a second instance type was the right call.

Next: NAT Gateways, Internet Gateways, and the route tables that actually wire all of this together. Right now half of what we've built only works because everything's still sharing that one flat route table from the default VPC. We're about to change that for real.

— Priya

tasks.question: Why does AWS strongly recommend spreading production resources across at least 2 Availability Zones, even though it costs more than running everything in one?
options: A) It's purely a billing requirement — AWS charges less per instance when spread across AZs

B) A single AZ is a physically separate facility (power, cooling, network) from other AZs in the same region — if that one facility has an outage, everything inside it goes down together, regardless of how well-architected the application itself is
C) Spreading across AZs is only relevant for compliance certifications, not actual reliability
D) AZs within a region share the same physical infrastructure, so spreading across them doesn't meaningfully reduce risk

C) All data since the last manual backup is lost, and the database must be restored from a snapshot
D) Multi-AZ only protects against data loss, not availability — the application still goes down until someone manually intervenes

tasks.scenario: You're about to enable Multi-AZ on foodquick-orders-db. karthik-dev asks: 'Does this mean we now have 2 separate databases we need to keep in sync ourselves, like a read replica setup?'
tasks.question: How should you correct this misunderstanding?
options: A) Yes — the team will need to write custom replication logic to keep both copies in sync

B) No — Multi-AZ is not the same as a read replica. AWS manages a synchronous standby copy automatically; the team never queries it directly, never manages replication, and only interacts with the single primary endpoint. It exists purely for automatic failover, not for read scaling.
C) Yes, but only during the first 24 hours after enabling it — after that, AWS merges the two copies back into one
D) No — Multi-AZ and read replicas are actually the exact same feature, just with different names in the console

tasks.scenario: You raise the ASG's desired count from 1 to 2. Priya asks a follow-up: 'If I set min=2 and desired=2 spanning 2 AZs, is that now actually safe against losing one AZ?'
tasks.question: Is min=2/desired=2 across exactly 2 AZs genuinely safe against one AZ failing?
options: A) Yes — with 2 AZs and desired=2, AWS guarantees exactly one instance per AZ, so losing one AZ always leaves exactly one instance running

B) Not fully — AWS's placement isn't strictly guaranteed to be perfectly 1-per-AZ, and even if it were, losing an AZ still means order-service drops to whatever's running in the surviving AZ alone, with zero spare capacity for that period. A safer target is enough total capacity that losing one AZ still leaves comfortable headroom, not just "technically still running"
C) Yes, and it's also fully protected against traffic spikes during the outage, since ASG auto-scales instantly to any load
D) No — 2 AZs can never be safe, only 3+ AZs count as "real" redundancy under any circumstances

Real answer: enough TOTAL capacity spread wide enough, so losing one AZ still leaves genuine headroom, not just bare survival.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — 'survives' and 'survives comfortably with headroom' are different bars. This real production thinking.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit simplistic you thought. Bare minimum 'still running' oda meaning not 'actually handling load comfortably'.

tasks.scenario: To validate the fix, you simulate an AZ failure by terminating the instance in ap-south-1b and watching the ASG try to replace capacity. It attempts to launch a replacement instance of the same type (m5.large) back into ap-south-1b.
tasks.error_shown: An error occurred (InsufficientInstanceCapacity) when calling the RunInstances operation: We currently do not have sufficient m5.large capacity in the Availability Zone you requested (ap-south-1b). Our system will be working on provisioning additional capacity.
tasks.diagnosis: Even with a correctly-configured Multi-AZ setup, AWS itself does not guarantee unlimited capacity of a specific instance type in every AZ at every moment — during real regional stress events (which is exactly when AZ failures tend to happen), a popular instance type can genuinely run short in one AZ. Relying on only 2 AZs and a single instance type means a real AZ failure can coincide with exactly this kind of capacity crunch, defeating the resilience design.
tasks.fix: Configure the ASG to span a third AZ (ap-south-1c is already available in this VPC) so there's another AZ to absorb capacity, and use a mixed instance types configuration (e.g. allow m5.large OR m5a.large OR m5n.large) so the ASG can launch whichever type has available capacity instead of being locked to one exact type.
tasks.explanation: This real, non-obvious operational lesson — Multi-AZ design you all did — thinking irundha, but specific instance type + specific AZ for combination capacity is not guaranteed. Real resilience —, AZ count only not, instance type flexibility also sernthu vendum.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks for the business case in numbers before approving the Multi-AZ change: what does it actually cost, versus what's the risk if FoodQuick skips it? FoodQuick's db.m5.large RDS instance costs roughly ₹28,000/month single-AZ; enabling Multi-AZ roughly doubles that instance cost to about ₹56,000/month. Separately, FoodQuick's lunch-hour peak processes around 3,200 orders/hour at an average order value of ₹280.
tasks.question: How should this be framed for Ravi, in real numbers?
tasks.solution: The Multi-AZ premium costs an extra ~₹28,000/month (~₹3.36 lakh/year). A single lost peak lunch hour of order-service downtime represents roughly 3,200 × ₹280 ≈ ₹8.96 lakh in that one hour alone — not counting customer trust or App Store review damage. The ₹28,000/month insurance cost is recovered by avoiding a small fraction of a single bad hour; skipping it to save money is a false economy the moment an AZ failure actually happens during peak hours.
tasks.explanation: This real business framing — cost of the fix vs cost of NOT fixing it, both real ₹ numbers's compare doing. ₹28,000/month insurance — , a peak hour downtime's ₹8.96 lakh risk's earlier microscopic is there.
